title: Three Doors Before War • The Woman Who Was Not Fighting • The Question in the Dark of Night • The Old Man, the Worshipper and the Fruit-Bearing Tree • Did You Split Open His Heart? • An Open Declaration Is Enough

blocks.1: In pre-Islamic Arabia there was no declaration of war. In the last watch of the night, the sound of horses’ hooves, then shouting. Waking up, one would find a tent on fire, another would see their herd of camels being driven off by men of another tribe. The opponent was not asked anything. What do you want, why have you come, is there any other way; there was no place for such questions. The sword was the first word, the sword was the last.
blocks.2: The Prophet {{1}} set an order even for war. When sending out any army he would tell the commander separately to fear Allah, and to treat his companions well. Then would come the matter of the enemy. Buraydah ibn al-Husayb (RA) remembered that instruction,
blocks.4: When you meet your enemy from among the polytheists, call them to three matters. Whichever of them they respond to, accept it, and hold your hand back from harming them. First call them to Islam; if they respond, accept it, hold back your hand. If they do not agree, ask them for the jizyah; if they agree to pay, accept it, hold back your hand. If they do not agree even to that, seek Allah’s help and fight them.{{1}}
blocks.5: Three doors. While the first two stood open, the third could not be touched. The sword was the last way, not the first. The aim of war was not to make anyone Muslim by force; it was the end of fitnah and oppression. The Qur’an has stated this limit of war like this,
blocks.7: Fight them until fitnah ends and the religion becomes Allah’s. Then if they desist, (know that) there should be no severity against anyone other than the wrongdoers.{{1}}
blocks.8: ‘If they desist’; with these few words war stops. For the one who has stopped, there is no permission to raise a hand. Severity is only for the wrongdoer. We often pick the harshest word in the very first sentence; at home, at work, in arguments. Yet even the one into whose hand the sword was placed was told to open two doors first. Before saying the hard word, have I kept the two gentle paths open!
blocks.9: Not a Wish to Meet the Enemy
blocks.10: On one expedition, as they waited before the enemy, the sun began to decline. The Prophet {{1}} stood among the Companions and said,
blocks.12: O people, do not wish for meeting the enemy; ask Allah for safety. But when you do meet them, be steadfast. And know that Paradise is beneath the shade of swords.{{1}}
blocks.13: The one who is the bravest is the very one saying, do not wish for war. Bravery does not mean seeking out fights; it means not turning back when a fight comes. Those in whose hands power rests often look for a chance to show it. The Prophet {{1}} taught that asking for safety is itself the real asking. Let there be strength; but let there be no need for it.
blocks.14: The Woman Who Was Not Fighting
blocks.15: On one expedition, people were standing in a crowd at one place. The Prophet {{1}} sent someone, go and see what the crowd is. He came back and said, a woman lies killed. At the head of the army was Khalid ibn al-Walid (RA). The Prophet {{2}} spoke; then he sent someone to Khalid,
blocks.17: This one was not someone to fight! … Go and tell Khalid, let him not kill any woman, nor any hired labourer.{{1}}
blocks.18: The word ‘asif’ means a hired labourer. The man who has come with the army to tend camels, draw water, carry loads; no sword in his hand. The measure of the prohibition is a question: was this one fighting? To make a target of one who is not fighting is forbidden. The general prohibition on killing women and children came in dars fourteen. Here came its reason, from the Prophet’s {{1}} own mouth.{{2}}
blocks.19: In anger we too punish wholesale. A whole family for one person’s fault, a whole department for one employee’s mistake. Even on the battlefield the Prophet {{1}} told them to look separately at who had raised a hand and who had not.
blocks.20: The Question in the Dark of Night
blocks.21: At al-Abwa’ or Waddan the Prophet {{1}} was passing by Sa‘b ibn Jaththamah (RA). There a question was put to him. Sa‘b (RA) remembered the question and the answer,
blocks.23: He was asked about the settlement of the polytheists that is raided at night, in which their women and children also get hurt. He said, they too are counted among them.{{1}}
blocks.24: In the earlier scene the Prophet {{1}} was angry on seeing the slain woman. Here he said, they too are counted among them. Put side by side, the two statements seem opposite to each other. They are not opposite. The questions are different.
blocks.25: In the case of the slain woman the question was whether one may kill by making someone a target. The answer: not one who is not fighting. Sa‘b’s question is another. A raid in the darkness of night. All asleep, who is who, no way to tell. The targets were fighters. But in the same house a mother sleeps, a child sleeps. What if they are hurt in the raid? The answer: in that situation they are counted, in ruling, with their fathers. For those who were hurt unintentionally while reaching the fathers, the responsibility was not placed on the raider. Unintentionally. Everything is in this one word. Nowhere in this hadith is there permission to knowingly target a woman or a child.{{1}}
blocks.26: Al-Zuhri (may Allah have mercy on him) said at the end of the hadith, after this the Prophet {{1}} forbade the killing of women and children. The prohibition and this answer come together at one place. Not on purpose; not if recognised. If a blow lands within an unavoidable mixing, there is no fault. And if someone knowingly kills one whom it was forbidden to kill? No diyah (blood-money) or kaffarah (expiation) falls upon him; what comes is the duty of repentance (tawbah) and seeking forgiveness (istighfar).{{2}}
blocks.27: When the Prophet {{1}} himself reached any settlement at night, he waited until dawn. That event will come in dars twenty-one. Many decisions we make in half-darkness; not all the information is at hand. Then what matters is to keep the intention clear, and not to give up even the effort to avoid the harm that can be avoided.
blocks.28: The Old Man, the Worshipper and the Fruit-Bearing Tree
blocks.29: After the Prophet’s {{1}} passing, the Caliph Abu Bakr (RA) sent several armies toward Sham. The commander of one was Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan. The army set out. The commander on horseback; the Caliph was walking beside him. Yazid said, either you mount, or I get down. Abu Bakr (RA) said, you will not get down, and I will not mount; I am counting these steps in the way of Allah. Then he said,
blocks.31: On the way you will find some people who think they have shut themselves away for Allah; leave them to that for which they have shut themselves away. … And I advise you with ten things. Do not kill any woman, any child, any decrepit old man. Do not cut a fruit-bearing tree. Do not ruin an inhabited settlement. Do not slaughter any goat or camel except for the need to eat. Do not burn a beehive, nor drown it. Do not misappropriate the spoils of war. And do not be a coward.{{1}}
blocks.32: After the Prophet {{1}}, the first Caliph, the first large army. And his first words were not about how to defeat the enemy; but about whom may not be touched. A person who has shut himself away in a house of worship, a decrepit old man, a fruit-bearing tree, a beehive. In the reckoning of war these have no value; for exactly that reason they are named separately. The jurists have put the crippled and the blind in this list too. The reason is one: permission for war is because of fighting, and these are not people of fighting.{{2}}
blocks.34: Yet at the siege of Banu al-Nadir some palm trees were cut and burned on the Prophet’s {{1}} own order; the Qur’an gave permission for it too. That event is in dars seventeen. Then what is the rule? The rule is: destruction is not the aim. When the enemy makes the orchard a shield, when there is no way to break the siege except cutting trees, then permission is by the measure of need. And when victory is nearly certain, the same act is disliked; because it is needless destruction.{{2}}
blocks.35: When power comes into the hand there is a pull to finish off everything of the opponent. After a quarrel, dragging up all the old words; in business, sinking the rival completely. Even on the battlefield, the army that had been told to remember the beehive, how can its successors snatch away even someone’s last belonging!
blocks.36: Did You Split Open His Heart?
blocks.37: An expedition went toward the Huraqah branch of the Juhaynah tribe. Attack at dawn; the enemy fell back. Usamah ibn Zayd (RA) and an Ansari pursued a man. As soon as they surrounded him the man cried out, la ilaha illa Allah. The Ansari drew back his hand. Usamah (RA) thrust his spear; the man died. Usamah; the son of one dear to the Prophet {{1}}, himself dear. After returning to Madinah the matter came up before the Prophet {{2}}. Usamah (RA) himself said,
blocks.39: He said, he said la ilaha illa Allah, and you killed him? I said, O Messenger of Allah, he only said it out of fear of the weapon. He said, did you split open his heart, so that you could know whether he said it from the heart or not? He kept repeating the words before me; in the end I felt, if only I had accepted Islam today!{{1}}
blocks.40: A beloved person; yet that day love gave no concession. One question, again and again. Miqdad ibn al-Aswad (RA) once came with an even harder question,
blocks.42: O Messenger of Allah, suppose I fight one of the disbelievers; he strikes my hand with the sword and cuts one off, then takes refuge behind a tree and says, I have submitted to Allah. After he has said this, should I kill him? He said, do not kill him. … If you kill him, he will be in the position you were in before you killed him; and you will be in the position he was in before he said the words he said.{{1}}
blocks.43: Even the man whose hand was cut off is safe once he says the Kalimah. Even with the greatest excuse for revenge in hand. Just such an incident happened on another expedition. A man with a small flock of goats; seeing the Muslims, he gave the salam. They thought, he is giving salam to save his life; they killed him and took the flock. The Qur’an then said it like this,
blocks.45: O you who believe! When you travel in the way of Allah, investigate carefully. Do not say to one who offers you the salam, ‘You are not a believer,’ out of desire for the goods of worldly life. For with Allah are abundant spoils. You too were like this before. Then Allah favoured you. So investigate carefully. Surely Allah is fully aware of all that you do.{{1}}
blocks.46: ‘You too were like this before.’ One day for you too Islam was only a declaration of the mouth; and only that much was counted enough for you. We read people’s intentions very quickly. That one gave charity to show off; that one took up prayer for gain. The Prophet’s {{1}} question is as sharp today; did you split open his heart!
blocks.48: A basic principle came out of the incident of Usamah (RA). The Prophet {{1}} stated it like this,
blocks.50: Whoever prays our prayer, faces our qiblah, eats our slaughtered animal, he is the Muslim; for him is the covenant of Allah and the covenant of His Messenger. So do not betray Allah in the covenant He has given.{{1}}
blocks.51: As long as revelation was descending, sometimes from the sky itself someone’s mask would be removed. After the Prophet {{1}} that door is shut. ‘Umar (RA) therefore said,
blocks.53: In the time of the Messenger of Allah {{1}} some people were taken to account through revelation. Now revelation has stopped. Now we will take you to account by your outward deeds. Whoever shows us good, we will keep him safe, draw him near; nothing of his inner self is our concern, the reckoning of the inner is for Allah to take.{{2}}
blocks.54: The outward is in people’s hands; the inward is in Allah’s hand. When this division gets confused, a person sits down in Allah’s seat.
blocks.55: Calling One’s Own Brother a Disbeliever
blocks.56: The reverse side of this is even more frightening. The Prophet {{1}} said,
blocks.58: If anyone says to his brother, O disbeliever, then the word will surely return upon one of the two.{{1}}
blocks.59: In another hadith it says that to accuse a believer of kufr is like killing him.{{1}}
blocks.60: Takfir means the ruling that puts someone out of Islam. After it, blood, property, marriage, funeral prayer; the reckoning of everything changes. So this ruling is not for emotion, not for a party; it is for deep knowledge and careful judgment.
blocks.61: At any difference of opinion we stick labels. This one is an innovator, that one is astray, that one is outside Islam itself. A word that can come back and land on oneself needs to be weighed twice before it leaves the mouth.

footnotes.0: Sahih Muslim 1731 (Kitab al-Jihad wa al-Siyar; from Buraydah ibn al-Husayb (RA)). The full text includes the part in between about migrating (hijrah) after accepting Islam or remaining in Bedouin status, and the part about the covenant (dhimmah) and judgment concerning the people of fortresses (the latter part is in the footnote to the section ‘The Line Between Strategy and Deception’ in this dars). Sunan Abi Dawud 2613 (al-Albani: sahih). The Arabic text of the hadith has the words ‘mina al-mushrikin’ (from among the polytheists); the quotation in the dars is a translation of just that. In Hanafi fiqh, among these three options, jizyah may be taken from the People of the Book (Arab or non-Arab), fire-worshippers and non-Arab polytheists; not from Arab polytheists, for whom it is either Islam or the sword (al-Kasani, Bada’i‘ al-Sana’i‘, Kitab al-Siyar, vol. 9, pp. 428, 433; evidence Tawbah 9:5 and 9:29).
footnotes.1: Tawdih al-Qur’an, vol. 1, Surah al-Baqarah 2:193, p. 120 (Taqi ‘Uthmani; checked against the rendered printed page). Note 123: in the Shari‘ah the aim of jihad is not to force anyone to accept Islam; in the ordinary situation, if anyone wants to remain firm in kufr, they can stay by showing respect for the law of the Islamic state through the jizyah (the ruling for the Arabian Peninsula is different).
footnotes.2: Sahih al-Bukhari 2965–2966, 3024–3025; Sahih Muslim 1742 (from ‘Abdullah ibn Abi Awfa (RA)). At the end of the hadith the Prophet’s {{1}} du‘a: ‘O Allah, Revealer of the Book, Mover of the clouds, Defeater of the combined armies, defeat them, help us.’
footnotes.3: Sunan Abi Dawud 2669 (from Rabah ibn al-Rabi‘ al-Usayyidi (RA), through his grandson ‘Umar ibn al-Murraqqi‘); al-Albani: hasan sahih; Silsilah Sahihah 701 (chain sahih); Sahih Ibn Hibban 4791 (Shu‘ayb al-Arna’ut: chain sahih). ‘Asif’ (‘asif) = a hired labourer or servant, who does not take part in the fighting.
footnotes.4: Sahih al-Bukhari 3014–3015 (from Ibn ‘Umar (RA); the prohibition of killing women and children on seeing the slain woman), quoted in dars 14.
footnotes.5: Sahih al-Bukhari 3012; Sahih Muslim 1745; Sunan Abi Dawud 2672; Musnad Ahmad 16426 (from Sa‘b ibn Jaththamah (RA); ‘the Prophet {{1}} passed by me at al-Abwa’ or Waddan; he was asked…’). In the text of al-Bukhari the questioner has no name (‘su’ila’, he was asked); in the text of Musnad Ahmad Sa‘b himself asked.
footnotes.6: Ibn Hajar, Fath al-Bari, commentary on 3012 (Salafiyyah edition, Kitab al-Jihad; PDF no. 07 in your folder, printed pp. 147–148): ‘hum minhum’ means ‘in that situation in terms of ruling’; the intention is not to indicate permission to kill women and children by targeting them (‘bi-tariq al-qasd’). The intention is: if there is no way to reach the fathers without trampling over them, and they get hurt because of being mixed in, then that is permissible. ‘Bayat’ means a night raid in such a way that individuals cannot be told apart. ‘Amr ibn Dinar understood the words as ‘they are with their fathers’ (Sunan Abi Dawud 2672). The statement ‘after this the Prophet {{1}} forbade the killing of women and children’ is al-Zuhri’s, not the Prophet’s {{2}} own words; as for the words ‘day of Hunayn’ added in Ibn Hibban’s narration, Ibn Hajar called it an addition by the narrator (‘mudraj’), and called the hadith of Rabah ibn al-Rabi‘ (Abu Dawud 2669) a supporter of this later prohibition. Some have taken Sa‘b’s hadith as abrogated on the basis of al-Zuhri’s statement; al-Hazimi said the opposite, that Sa‘b’s hadith itself abrogated the prohibition hadiths, which Ibn Hajar called ‘gharib’. Most scholars have reconciled the two: this is the view of al-Shafi‘i and the jurists of Kufah. The view of Malik and al-Awza‘i is stricter still: even if they are used as a shield, women and children may not be targeted.
footnotes.7: Al-Kasani, Bada’i‘ al-Sana’i‘, Kitab al-Siyar (vol. 9; PDF no. 10 in the folder): p. 393: ‘there is no harm in a surprise night raid and bayat’ (‘wa la ba’sa bi-l-bayat’). p. 400: if one (knowingly) kills any of those whose killing is not lawful, there is no diyah or kaffarah, only tawbah and istighfar; because the legal value of an unbeliever’s blood is not fixed without aman (safe-conduct). Editorial note on p. 398: that the killing of women and children is forbidden if they do not fight, the jurists agree. The Prophet’s {{1}} arriving at night and waiting until dawn: Sahih al-Bukhari 610 (dars 21).
footnotes.8: Muwatta’ Imam Malik, Kitab al-Jihad, Bab al-Nahy ‘an Qatl al-Nisa’ wa al-Wildan, no. 982 (from Yahya ibn Sa‘id, without a connected chain up to Abu Bakr (RA); the dialogue of walking is in the wording ‘za‘amu’, that is, ‘people say’). Shu‘ayb al-Arna’ut, Takhrij Sharh al-Sunnah 2696: ‘the narrators are trustworthy, but the chain is broken (munqati‘)’; al-Bayhaqi, Ma‘rifat al-Sunan 18075–18078: through several broken chains; Ibn Kathir, Irshad al-Faqih 2/320: ‘narrated from Abu Bakr (RA) through many chains’. This is not a hadith of the Prophet {{1}}, it is the Caliph’s advice (athar); the jurists accepted it because its content is consistent with the sahih hadiths (Abu Dawud 2669; Bukhari 3014–3015). The reading ‘nahlan’ (bees) is the Muwatta’s (the original text checked); in some narrations, including in Ibn Kathir’s quotation, ‘nakhlan’ (palm trees). The part in the middle that was omitted (about a group of fighters with the middle of the head shaved) is outside the subject of the dars.
footnotes.9: Al-Kasani, Bada’i‘ al-Sana’i‘ (Dar al-Kutub al-‘Ilmiyyah, edited by ‘Ali Mu‘awwad and ‘Adil ‘Abd al-Mawjud), Kitab al-Siyar, ‘Fasl fi Bayan Man Yahillu Qatluhu wa Man la Yahillu’, pp. 398–400: during fighting it is not lawful to kill women, children, decrepit old men, the crippled, those paralysed on one side, the blind, those with hands and feet cut off, the insane, monks in places of worship, hermits on mountains, and worshippers who stay in their homes with doors closed; ‘because these are not people of fighting’ (‘li’anna ha’ula’i laysu min ahl al-qital’). Principle: one who is a person of fighting, killing him is lawful; one who is not, only when he actually fights, or takes part in the fighting by giving counsel, obedience and incitement; even if a woman or child (at Hunayn the old Duraid ibn al-Simmah, whose counsel alone was of use, was killed, the Prophet {{1}} did not object).
footnotes.10: Surah al-Hashr 59:5; Sahih al-Bukhari 4031 (cutting and burning the palm trees of Banu al-Nadir), detailed in dars 17. Al-Kasani, Bada’i‘ al-Sana’i‘ (Dar al-Kutub al-‘Ilmiyyah, edited by ‘Ali Mu‘awwad and ‘Adil ‘Abd al-Mawjud), Kitab al-Siyar, pp. 393–394: there is no harm in cutting the enemy’s fruit-bearing and fruitless trees, destroying crops, burning or flooding fortresses, the evidence Hashr 59:5 and 59:2. But when victory is nearly certain it is makruh, because it is destruction beyond need: Ibn al-Humam, Fath al-Qadir (commentary on al-Hidayah), quoted in the note on the same page of Bada’i‘ al-Sana’i‘. ‘Ali Muhammad al-Sallabi, The Prophet’s Life of War (Bengali), p. 274 (‘Destroying the Enemy’s Wealth and Crops’).
footnotes.11: Sahih Muslim 96; Sahih al-Bukhari 4269, 6872 (from Usamah ibn Zayd (RA); the Huraqah expedition). ‘If only I had accepted Islam today’ means: then accepting Islam would have wiped out all previous sins, this mistake too (the Bukhari text: ‘if only I had not been Muslim before today’). Usamah is the son of Zayd ibn Harithah, the Prophet’s {{1}} freed slave and adopted son.
footnotes.12: Sahih al-Bukhari 4019; Sahih Muslim 95 (from Miqdad ibn al-Aswad (RA)); Sunan Abi Dawud 2644 (al-Albani: sahih).
footnotes.13: Tawdih al-Qur’an, vol. 1, Surah al-Nisa’ 4:94, pp. 270–271. Occasion of revelation: Sahih al-Bukhari 4591; Sahih Muslim 3025 (Ibn ‘Abbas (RA): the man with the flock of goats gave the salam, yet he was killed and the flock taken, then the verse was revealed). Tawdih note 59: if someone accepts Islam before us we shall consider them Muslim, the state of the heart is with Allah; note 60: ‘you too were like this before’, that is, there was no proof of your being Muslim other than a verbal declaration.
footnotes.14: Sahih al-Bukhari 391 (from Anas ibn Malik (RA)); in the same sense 393.
footnotes.15: Sahih al-Bukhari 2641 (from ‘Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA)). The end of the text: ‘And whoever shows us evil, we shall not consider him safe, nor trust him, even if he says that his inside is good.’
footnotes.17: Sahih al-Bukhari 6105, 6652 (from Thabit ibn al-Dahhak (RA)): ‘To accuse a believer of kufr is like killing him.’

quiz.q: What did the Prophet ﷺ tell the army’s commander to call the enemy to first?
o: To the jizyah
To Islam
To a truce
To aman (safe-conduct)
quiz.e: The first door is Islam, then jizyah, then fighting (Sahih Muslim 1731).

quiz.q: Which Companion remembered the instruction the Prophet ﷺ gave to the commander?
o: al-Nu‘man ibn Muqarrin (RA)
Abu Usayd al-Sa‘idi (RA)
Buraydah ibn al-Husayb (RA)
Sa‘b ibn Jaththamah al-Laythi (RA)
quiz.e: Sahih Muslim 1731, from Buraydah (RA).

quiz.q: In the hadith ‘do not wish to meet the enemy’, where is Paradise said to be?
o: Beneath the feet of mothers
In the drops of the martyr’s blood
In the field of shooting arrows
Beneath the shade of swords
quiz.e: ‘Know that Paradise is beneath the shade of swords’ (Sahih al-Bukhari 2966).

quiz.q: What can be understood about the aim of war from the ‘three doors’?
o: The aim is to annihilate the enemy completely
Gaining spoils is the main aim
Forcing people to become Muslim is not the aim
Taking revenge is the real aim
quiz.e: That the jizyah door is open proves that the aim is the end of fitnah and oppression (Tawdih, note on 2:193).

quiz.q: ‘Do not wish to meet the enemy’ and ‘be steadfast when you meet them’; together, what definition of bravery do they make?
o: Always being eager for fighting
Proposing a truce on seeing the enemy
Avoiding the field for safety
Not seeking fights, not turning back if one comes
quiz.e: Asking for safety is the real asking; but steadfastness when the fight comes.

quiz.q: What does the lesson of the ‘three doors’ say when there is a difference of opinion at the office?
o: Keep the gentle paths open before harsh words
Say the harshest word at the very start
Quietly withdraw when there is a difference
Report directly to the authority
quiz.e: Even the swordsman was told to open two doors first.

quiz.q: On seeing the slain woman, whom did the Prophet ﷺ send word to Khalid (RA) not to kill?
o: Women and hired labourers
The old and worshippers
Women and blind people equally
The crippled and children
quiz.e: ‘Tell Khalid, let him not kill any woman, nor any hired labourer’ (Abu Dawud 2669).

quiz.q: What does the word ‘asif’ mean?
o: A decrepit old man
A hired labourer
A person engaged in worship
An adviser in war
quiz.e: ‘Asif: a hired labourer who comes with the army, with no sword in his hand.

quiz.q: From the statement ‘This one was not someone to fight!’, what is the measure of the prohibition on killing?
o: Whether the person is taking part in the fighting
Which tribe the person belongs to
Whether the person is from the Muslims’ enemy side
Whether the person has wealth
quiz.e: In Hanafi fiqh too the basis of permission to kill is fighting (al-hirab).

quiz.q: Punishing a whole department for one employee’s mistake goes against which lesson?
o: Saving the arrows
Looking separately at who has raised a hand
News first, then the foot
What my man gives as word is my word
quiz.e: Seeing the slain woman, the Prophet ﷺ separated fighter from non-fighter.

quiz.q: Where was the question about the night raid asked?
o: On the road to Badr at Harrat al-Wabarah
At Wadi al-Qura
At al-Abwa’ or Waddan
On the Huraqah expedition
quiz.e: Sa‘b (RA) said that the Prophet ﷺ was passing by him at al-Abwa’ or Waddan (Sahih al-Bukhari 3012).

quiz.q: How do the hadith of the slain woman and Sa‘b’s hadith ‘they too are counted among them’ fit together?
o: Making them a target is forbidden, hurt from unintended mixing is different
Sa‘b’s hadith gives a general permission to kill women and children
The hadith of the slain woman applies only to one particular expedition
The contradiction between the two remains, so one has to be taken as abrogated
quiz.e: The two questions are different: killing by targeting, and a blow landing in unavoidable mixing in a night raid (Ibn Hajar).

quiz.q: ‘They too are counted among them’; this answer is about what kind of harm?
o: Knowingly and deliberately targeting women and children
Hurt that lands unintentionally in the dark
Treatment of captive women
Cutting the enemy’s fruit-bearing trees
quiz.e: The prohibition on intentional killing is separate; the question is about harm that cannot be avoided.

quiz.q: If one has to make a big decision with incomplete information, what is the dars’s lesson?
o: Do nothing until all the information is had
Whatever harm results, place the responsibility fully on others
Keep the intention clear and avoid the harm that can be avoided
Bring quick results by any means
quiz.e: The lesson of the question in the dark of night.

quiz.q: Beside which commander was Abu Bakr (RA) walking on the road to Sham?
o: Khalid ibn al-Walid
Mu‘awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan
Usamah ibn Zayd
Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan
quiz.e: Commander on horse, Caliph on foot; when Yazid wanted to get down he spoke of counting the steps in Allah’s way.

quiz.q: What does Abu Bakr’s (RA) advice forbid burning or drowning?
o: A beehive
The enemy’s fortress
An inhabited settlement
The spoils of war
quiz.e: ‘Do not burn a beehive, nor drown it.’

quiz.q: What is the status of Abu Bakr’s (RA) advice?
o: A connected hadith of the Prophet ﷺ
A direct explanation of a Qur’anic verse
The Caliph’s advice, with a broken chain
A sahih marfu‘ narration of al-Bukhari
quiz.e: In the Muwatta’ with a broken chain; its content is consistent with sahih hadiths.

quiz.q: The cutting of Banu al-Nadir’s palm trees and ‘do not cut a fruit-bearing tree’; what is the resolution?
o: The later command abrogated the earlier
Only in the Caliph’s time did tree-cutting become forbidden
Both are part of a general permission
Permission when needed, not without need
quiz.e: When victory is nearly certain, cutting trees is makruh; because it is needless destruction (al-Hidayah).

quiz.q: Against the tendency to sink a rival completely in business, which picture stands opposite?
o: The man who said the Kalimah behind a tree
That chief of Yamamah tied to the mosque pillar
The night raid on a settlement in the dark
Remembering the beehive even on a war march
quiz.e: Not snatching away anyone’s last possession even when power is in hand.

quiz.q: Which expedition was Usamah’s (RA) incident from?
o: The expedition of the Najd cavalry
The Huraqah expedition of Juhaynah
The expedition on the road to Badr
The expedition of Wadi al-Qura
quiz.e: An expedition toward the Huraqah branch of the Juhaynah tribe (Sahih Muslim 96).

quiz.q: Who asked about the man who said the Kalimah after his hand was cut off?
o: Usamah ibn Zayd (RA)
Sa‘b ibn Jaththamah (RA)
Miqdad ibn al-Aswad (RA)
Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman (RA)
quiz.e: Sahih al-Bukhari 4019; Muslim 95.

quiz.q: In the occasion of revelation of verse 94 of Surah al-Nisa’, what had the man done?
o: Said the Kalimah
Hid behind a tree
Wanted to pay the jizyah
Gave the salam
quiz.e: The man with the flock of goats gave the salam (Sahih al-Bukhari 4591).

quiz.q: What is the main lesson of the question ‘Did you split open his heart?’
o: Judgment of the heart is not in people’s hands
The Kalimah has no value in war
A Kalimah said out of fear of weapons is not acceptable
A dear one’s mistake should be forgiven
quiz.e: An open declaration is enough; the inward reckoning is Allah’s.

quiz.q: In Miqdad’s question, what is the significance of ‘you will go to his position’?
o: Gaining the right to take revenge for the cut hand
By killing a safe Muslim one’s own blood becomes claimable
The man who said the Kalimah remaining a disbeliever
One can become entitled to reward by taking revenge for the cut hand
quiz.e: After the Kalimah he is safe; if killed, the killer is responsible.

quiz.q: ‘You too were like this before’; according to the Tawdih al-Qur’an note, what does it mean?
o: You too were prisoners of war before
You too once fought only out of greed for spoils
Your Islam too was accepted on a verbal declaration
You too used to receive heavenly news before
quiz.e: Note 60: there was no proof of your being Muslim other than a verbal declaration.

quiz.q: When someone gives charity, saying ‘he did it to show off’ stands before which question?
o: Did you split open his heart?
Was this one fighting, or not fighting?
Thumamah, what do you have, tell me?
What happened, why are you not shooting arrows?
quiz.e: We do not have the right to read intentions.

quiz.q: ‘Now we will take you to account by your outward deeds’; whose statement is it?
o: ‘Umar’s (RA)
Abu Bakr’s (RA)
‘Ali’s (RA)
Mu‘awiyah’s (RA)
quiz.e: Sahih al-Bukhari 2641.

quiz.q: Why did ‘Umar (RA) say that now people will be taken to account only by outward deeds?
o: Because there are no more hypocrites
As a new policy of the caliphate
Because the number of judges is small
Because revelation has stopped
quiz.e: In the Prophet’s ﷺ time some people were taken through revelation; now revelation has stopped.

quiz.q: Which hadith is important to remember before declaring someone ‘outside Islam’ over a difference of opinion?
o: The Muslims’ covenant is one, even an ordinary person can give it
The word ‘disbeliever’ returns upon one of the two
War is strategy
Strength is shooting arrows
quiz.e: Sahih al-Bukhari 6104; and accusing a believer of kufr is like killing him (6105).
